   In the U.S. and a few other countries, surging investments in AI are helping mask the financial pain of higher costs, triggered in part by the Iran war and its widening fallout. But elsewhere, popular discontent is boiling over as governments get caught between spending more to help their citizens and servicing their spiraling debts.

   In France, high-school and university students are protesting plans by the government to cut spending amid a selloff in the nation’s debt. Transport drivers in the Philippines and Indonesia have in recent weeks taken to the streets over high gas and diesel prices. Senegal last month alerted international bondholders and Chinese state-owned banks that it would need debt relief.

   The International Monetary Fund, whose annual meetings in Bangkok this week bring together the world’s finance ministers and central bankers, says it expects the global economy to grow 3.1% this year, down from 3.5% in 2025.

   Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

       Planning & Investing   Rising Rates Threaten Wall Street’s Golden Goose in Trading   Weak bond markets undermine what had been a strength for big banks. 

       Market Talk   From Dow Jones Newswires 

   Canadian manufacturing sales rebounded in August but not as strongly as the headlines might suggest, says Capital Economics’ Thomas Ryan. The economist says the 1.5% rise on-month was purely down to price effects, with sales volumes unchanged as new U.S. section 338 tariffs began to weigh on the factory sector. Added to a drop in wholesale trade volumes for the month and it suggests downside risk to the preliminary estimate that GDP rose 0.2% on-month in August, Ryan says. And that reinforces Capital’s forecast the Bank of Canada will deliver only two of the roughly four rate increases currently priced in by markets. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

   The northeastern Spanish region of Catalonia is expected to grow faster than Madrid for the first time in six years, BBVA economists say. The bank expects Catalonia’s economy to expand 2.3% in 2027, boosted especially by improved goods exports, while Madrid region is expected to grow 2.1%. Catalonia, with its bigger population and industrial base, historically had a larger economy than Madrid, but its GDP was overtaken by the capital’s in 2017. The two regions account for the highest share of the Spanish economy, and both will continue to benefit from services exports, including tourism. BBVA expects Spanish GDP growth to slow to 2.1% next year, from 2.6% in 2026, as high energy prices, inflation and elevated interest rates damp activity. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

RUNGROJ YONGRIT/EPA/SHUTTERSTOCK
 

Economic damage from high energy prices and rising borrowing costs is mounting globally, splitting the world into a new set of winners and losers as countries with limited exposure to the artificial-intelligence boom fall behind.

 

In the U.S. and a few other countries, surging investments in AI are helping mask the financial pain of higher costs, triggered in part by the Iran war and its widening fallout. But elsewhere, popular discontent is boiling over as governments get caught between spending more to help their citizens and servicing their spiraling debts.

 

In France, high-school and university students are protesting plans by the government to cut spending amid a selloff in the nation’s debt. Transport drivers in the Philippines and Indonesia have in recent weeks taken to the streets over high gas and diesel prices. Senegal last month alerted international bondholders and Chinese state-owned banks that it would need debt relief.

 

The International Monetary Fund, whose annual meetings in Bangkok this week bring together the world’s finance ministers and central bankers, says it expects the global economy to grow 3.1% this year, down from 3.5% in 2025.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

Canadian manufacturing sales rebounded in August but not as strongly as the headlines might suggest, says Capital Economics’ Thomas Ryan. The economist says the 1.5% rise on-month was purely down to price effects, with sales volumes unchanged as new U.S. section 338 tariffs began to weigh on the factory sector. Added to a drop in wholesale trade volumes for the month and it suggests downside risk to the preliminary estimate that GDP rose 0.2% on-month in August, Ryan says. And that reinforces Capital’s forecast the Bank of Canada will deliver only two of the roughly four rate increases currently priced in by markets. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

 

The northeastern Spanish region of Catalonia is expected to grow faster than Madrid for the first time in six years, BBVA economists say. The bank expects Catalonia’s economy to expand 2.3% in 2027, boosted especially by improved goods exports, while Madrid region is expected to grow 2.1%. Catalonia, with its bigger population and industrial base, historically had a larger economy than Madrid, but its GDP was overtaken by the capital’s in 2017. The two regions account for the highest share of the Spanish economy, and both will continue to benefit from services exports, including tourism. BBVA expects Spanish GDP growth to slow to 2.1% next year, from 2.6% in 2026, as high energy prices, inflation and elevated interest rates damp activity. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)
